question: the economic, financial, and industrial technologies of narcotics empires, from the historical cases through their continuation into the modern era, treated as a value chain from territory to population
method: web research from first-party and scholarly surfaces by a researcher given the question and no context of the house or its goals (founder-ordered 2026-09-05); every figure carries its source URL, title, and access date; contested figures carry both figures
commissionedBy: the executive session of 2026-09-05 (bare-cedar-fog, session b72aec4f), for the territorial-economy program carrier
notFound: a manufacturing cost per OxyContin pill
a quantified pharmacy-benefit-manager markup or rebate specific to OxyContin
a single uncontested Sinaloa annual revenue figure
a heroin-specific risk-compensation share of retail price in the Caulkins and Reuter literature
scholarly literature using the exact phrase digital opium for short-video platforms (adjacent terms found: spiritual opium, electronic opium, electronic fentanyl, electronic cocaine)

rows.case: British East India Company opium trade / Opium Wars
rows.claim: The East India Company secured an opium monopoly in Bengal in 1773, requiring cultivators to bring all opium to Company warehouses (godowns), fostering cultivation through loans/bonuses to growers rather than open-market purchase.
rows.sourceTitle: Opium - Captions, Cambridge University Library

rows.case: British East India Company opium trade / Opium Wars
rows.claim: The Company extended its opium monopoly to include Bombay opium in 1830, broadening the geographic base of controlled cultivation.
rows.sourceTitle: Opium Trading in Mumbai, Wikipedia
rows.note: Wikipedia used as secondary source; corroborated by Cambridge Library captions page.

rows.claim: Colombian coca farmers sell raw coca leaf for about $400-500 per ton; farmers who process leaf into coca base/paste themselves can get about $900 per kilogram of paste.
rows.sourceTitle: Legendary drug lord Pablo Escobar lost $2.1 billion in cash each year — and it didn't matter, Yahoo Finance
rows.note: Article discusses supply-chain pricing generally, not only historical Escobar era.

rows.claim: Colombian cocaine hydrochloride (HCl) yield per hectare of coca rose from 6.5 kg/ha in 2016 to 7.9 kg/ha in 2020, a 23% increase, attributed to more intensive cultivation and higher-yielding coca strains.
rows.unit: kg cocaine HCl per hectare per year
rows.sourceTitle: Challenging the Cocaine Figures, Part II: Colombia, InSight Crime (citing UNODC data)

rows.claim: The wholesale price paid to Mexican marijuana growers fell from $60-90 per kilogram to $30-40 per kilogram as U.S. state-level legalization expanded, undercutting cartel-linked cannabis cultivation.
rows.sourceTitle: Legal Pot In The U.S. May Be Undercutting Mexican Marijuana, NPR

rows.case: Golden Triangle and Afghan opium economies
rows.claim: Shan State accounts for 92% of Myanmar's opium poppy cultivation, making it the dominant growing region in the Golden Triangle.
rows.sourceTitle: Myanmar remains the world's leading source of opium and heroin, UNODC

rows.case: Golden Triangle and Afghan opium economies
rows.claim: In Kachin State, Myanmar, poppy-growing farmers earned on average $584 from their opium crop versus $336 earned by non-poppy farmers growing other crops.
rows.sourceTitle: Opium economy in Golden Triangle sees steady growth in 2023, UNODC

rows.case: Golden Triangle and Afghan opium economies
rows.claim: The average farm-gate price paid to Golden Triangle opium farmers rose 27% to about $355 per kilogram of dry opium in 2023.
rows.sourceTitle: Opium economy in Golden Triangle sees steady growth in 2023, UNODC

rows.case: Golden Triangle and Afghan opium economies
rows.claim: Afghan opium sold at an average farm-gate price of $63/kg in 2019; by August 2023 the average monthly farm-gate price of dried opium had risen to about $408/kg, following the Taliban's 2022 cultivation ban.
rows.sourceTitle: UNODC Research brief, Afghanistan opium survey 2023
rows.note: Contested/time-varying figure: prices differ sharply by year because of the intervening cultivation ban; both figures given rather than a single number.

rows.case: Golden Triangle and Afghan opium economies
rows.claim: Afghan opium yield per hectare has varied widely by year: 44.5 kg/ha (2011), 23.7 kg/ha (2012), 18.3 kg/ha (2015), 23.8 kg/ha (2016), 27.3 kg/ha (2017), 38.5 kg/ha (2021), 26.7 kg/ha (2022).
rows.sourceTitle: 2012 Afghanistan Opium Survey and related UNODC year-by-year survey releases
rows.note: Compiled across several UNODC annual survey press releases; single row aggregates multiple years for brevity.

rows.case: Golden Triangle and Afghan opium economies
rows.claim: In 2025, Afghanistan's area under opium poppy cultivation was estimated at 10,200 hectares, with potential opium production of about 296 tons, down 32% from 2024 -- reflecting continued enforcement of the Taliban's 2022 ban.
rows.sourceTitle: Afghanistan Opium Survey 2025, UNODC

rows.claim: Legal, licensed poppy-straw agriculture supplies the pharmaceutical opioid industry: Australia (mainly Tasmania), India and Turkey are the major legal producers, with U.S. manufacturers required to import 80% of narcotic raw material from India and Turkey; Tasmania grows a mutant thebaine/oripavine poppy (TOP1) used to manufacture oxycodone and buprenorphine.
rows.unit: percent of U.S. narcotic raw material import requirement
rows.sourceTitle: Welcome to the Australian Island That Fueled America's Opioid Crisis, Vice
rows.note: This is the licit-agriculture upstream input to OxyContin's active ingredient supply, distinct from the illicit poppy economies of Afghanistan/Golden Triangle.

rows.claim: Unlike opium- or coca-derived narcotics, fentanyl is a fully synthetic opioid with no agricultural cultivation step; its supply chain begins with chemical precursors rather than a farmed crop.
rows.sourceTitle: China Primer: Illicit Fentanyl and China's Role, Congressional Research Service
rows.note: Interpretation drawn from the source's description of a chemical-precursor supply chain; the source does not use the word 'agrarian' but describes no cultivation stage.

rows.case: British East India Company opium trade / Opium Wars
rows.claim: Opium imports into China grew from about 200 chests annually in 1729, to roughly 1,000 chests by 1767, to about 10,000 chests per year between 1820-1830, reaching about 40,000 chests annually by 1838.
rows.sourceTitle: Opium trade, Encyclopaedia Britannica

rows.case: British East India Company opium trade / Opium Wars
rows.claim: In the 1820s the opium trade averaged about nine hundred tons per year shipped from Bengal to China, processed and packed at Company warehouses before export by licensed private 'country traders'.
rows.sourceTitle: Opium Wars, New World Encyclopedia

rows.claim: Cocaine's farm-to-street price ladder in the 1980s-2010s ran roughly: coca leaf $400-500/ton -> coca paste $900/kg -> Colombian export-grade cocaine $10,000-20,000/kg -> U.S. wholesale $70,000-80,000/kg -> street-level (cut/diluted) equivalent of about $150,000/kg.
rows.unit: USD per kilogram across chain stages
rows.sourceTitle: Legendary drug lord Pablo Escobar lost $2.1 billion in cash each year — and it didn't matter, Yahoo Finance
rows.note: Figures reflect contemporary (not strictly 1980s-1990s Escobar-era) chain pricing, cited by the source as illustrative of the general markup structure.

rows.claim: In Colombia, a kilogram of cocaine sold at the farm-gate/export level for about $1,654 in 2018, rising to roughly $2,000 more recently -- while retail cocaine reaches up to $25,000/kg equivalent in the United States.
rows.sourceTitle: Colombia: average price of cocaine 2021, Statista

rows.claim: Mexican trafficking organizations obtain fentanyl precursor chemicals largely from China and India, imported through Mexico's Pacific gateway, with the port of Manzanillo the dominant point of unlading before onward domestic synthesis.
rows.sourceTitle: Precursors, Ports, and Pills: Inside the China-Mexico-U.S. Fentanyl Supply Chain, National Security Data and Policy Institute (University of Virginia)

rows.claim: The DEA assesses that Chinese traffickers have shifted from directly manufacturing and exporting finished fentanyl to instead exporting precursor chemicals to Mexican cartels, who now do the manufacturing; almost no finished fentanyl has been detected entering the U.S. directly from China since China imposed class-wide fentanyl-related-substance controls in 2019.
rows.sourceTitle: China Primer: Illicit Fentanyl and China's Role, Congressional Research Service

rows.claim: A pill press capable of producing 5,000 counterfeit pills per hour was found priced at $995, with die molds for oxycodone/Xanax-marked pills priced at $115-130 and punch/die kits available online for about $40; one kilogram of fentanyl powder can be pressed into hundreds of thousands of pills, generating an estimated $10-20 million in retail sales at $10-20 per pill.
rows.sourceTitle: Pill Press Fact Sheet, Legislative Analysis and Public Policy Association (citing DEA data)

rows.case: Golden Triangle and Afghan opium economies
rows.claim: About 60% of Afghan opium is processed domestically into morphine base/heroin using crude acid-base extraction laboratories; UNODC estimates roughly 475 metric tons of acetic anhydride (the key acetylating precursor) are smuggled into Afghanistan annually to support this processing.
rows.sourceTitle: Afghanistan opium/heroin production, GlobalSecurity.org (citing UNODC estimates)

rows.claim: The average U.S. wholesale price of a 30mg OxyContin capsule is approximately $7.75; specific manufacturing/production cost per pill for OxyContin was searched for but not found in public sources.
rows.sourceTitle: Drug prices and trends for OXYCONTIN, DrugPatentWatch
rows.note: Manufacturing/COGS-per-pill figure not found; see 'Not found' list.

rows.case: British East India Company opium trade / Opium Wars
rows.claim: Because direct Company sale of opium in China was illegal under Qing law, the Company sold opium at Calcutta auction to licensed private 'country traders,' who shipped it to the Chinese coast and sold it on to local smuggling networks -- separating the Company's monopoly from criminal liability for the final import.
rows.sourceTitle: Opium trade, Encyclopaedia Britannica

rows.case: British East India Company opium trade / Opium Wars
rows.claim: Rural Chinese opium dealers built a hierarchical shareholding distribution enterprise: founders who took a share of profits on all opium sold, presiding over investor-salesmen who in turn managed teams of transporters and retailers reaching inland consumers.
rows.sourceTitle: The Opium Business: Introduction, Stanford University Press

rows.claim: Over half of narco semi-submersibles/submarines are built in artisanal shipyards along Colombia's Pacific coast, correlated with cocaine-producing departments (Nariño, Cauca); vessels are launched toward Central America and Sinaloa-controlled areas of Mexico, with fishing boats used as countersurveillance escorts.
rows.unit: percent (approx. share of narco-sub construction on Colombia's Pacific coast)
rows.sourceTitle: Under the Radar: What Hundreds of Narco Sub Seizures Tell Us About Global Cocaine Routes, InSight Crime

rows.claim: Cocaine traffickers increasingly route product through commercial container shipping, preferring shippers/routes where goods change hands the fewest times to minimize the risk of discovery.
rows.sourceTitle: Fishing Boats and Cargo Ships: How Colombian Cocaine Travels the World, OCCRP

rows.claim: The Sinaloa Cartel uses a franchise-style 'plaza system,' dividing Mexico into territories ('plazas') each run by a jefe de plaza who manages security, logistics, and local corruption for that route and pays a percentage of earnings up to a central leadership 'board' -- compared explicitly by analysts to subsidiary/franchise corporate structures such as Walmart or McDonald's.
rows.sourceTitle: Journal of Strategic Security, Volume 15 Number 4, University of South Florida

rows.claim: Plaza bosses (jefes de plaza) hold considerable day-to-day operating autonomy over their territory, while top Sinaloa leadership prioritizes consensus-building among plaza bosses before major decisions such as starting a conflict or forming alliances.
rows.sourceTitle: How Mexico's Sinaloa Cartel Has Stayed United for Decades, InSight Crime

rows.claim: Fentanyl production in Mexico is now geographically concentrated, with Mexican manufacturing plants receiving precursor chemicals from overseas (China, India) and distributing finished product through established drug-transit networks into U.S. entry corridors -- described by researchers as one adaptive, single supply chain rather than separate trafficking and chemical-trade systems.
rows.sourceTitle: Precursors, Ports, and Pills: Inside the China-Mexico-U.S. Fentanyl Supply Chain, National Security Data and Policy Institute (University of Virginia)

rows.claim: Specific figures on OxyContin's wholesale-to-retail pharmacy distribution margins and the role of pharmacy benefit managers in that markup were searched for and not found in detail beyond a general statement that rebating/contracting with insurers and PBMs erodes most list-price increases.
rows.sourceTitle: Endo Pharmaceuticals Holdings Inc, Form 424B4 FY2005, SEC EDGAR
rows.note: Specific PBM markup percentage not found; see 'Not found' list.

rows.case: British East India Company opium trade / Opium Wars
rows.claim: The Treaty of Nanking (1842) imposed a war indemnity of 21 million taels of silver on the Qing government (roughly 27 million silver dollars), composed of 6 million for opium confiscated by Lin Zexu in 1839, 6 million for the 1841 Ransom of Canton, 3 million for merchant debts, and 12 million in war reparations, payable in installments at 5% annual interest on late payments.
rows.sourceTitle: Treaty of Nanking, Wikipedia

rows.case: British East India Company opium trade / Opium Wars
rows.claim: Opium revenue from Bengal and Bombay amounted to approximately five million pounds sterling per year at the trade's height, becoming the second-largest source of revenue for British India by 1843.
rows.sourceTitle: Opium - Captions, Cambridge University Library

rows.claim: Estimates of Medellín Cartel revenue vary enormously by methodology: one estimate puts peak revenue at about $420 million per week (~$21.8 billion annualized) or over $25 billion annually at its absolute peak; a lower estimate puts annual revenue at $2-4 billion.
rows.sourceTitle: Legendary drug lord Pablo Escobar lost $2.1 billion in cash each year — and it didn't matter, Yahoo Finance
rows.note: Contested figure: both low and high published estimates given because sources disagree by an order of magnitude.

rows.claim: At its peak, Medellín Cartel revenue was compared to Colombia's entire GDP, which stood at roughly $25-30 billion per year in the early 1980s.
rows.sourceTitle: Legendary drug lord Pablo Escobar lost $2.1 billion in cash each year — and it didn't matter, Yahoo Finance

rows.claim: The Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI) laundered money for the Medellín Cartel (as well as Saddam Hussein, Manuel Noriega, and Abu Nidal's network); its Tampa branch was investigated in the mid-1980s for laundering Medellín drug proceeds, and BCCI pleaded guilty in January 1990, paying a then-record $14.8 million fine for drug-money laundering.
rows.sourceTitle: The BCCI Collapse: Bank of Crooks and Criminals, 1972-1991, Market Histories

rows.claim: BCCI collapsed on 5 July 1991 when regulators in seven countries shut down the $20 billion lender, which had operated across 73 countries; a Price Waterhouse audit had revealed fraudulent concealment of huge losses.
rows.sourceTitle: The BCCI Affair - 4. BCCI's Criminality, U.S. Congress (Kerry-Brown Report)

rows.claim: Estimates of Colombian drug-money laundering as a share of GDP vary sharply by year and source: 10% of GDP in 1985, rising to 14% by the end of the 1990s, but reported by the Colombian government at about 2% of GDP in 2013; separately, one Andes University estimate put cocaine-trafficking's direct contribution to 2018 GDP at almost 2% (~$18.3 billion), while a White House estimate for the same period put it at just 0.4% of GDP.
rows.sourceTitle: 'Money Laundering 2% of Colombia GDP', InSight Crime
rows.note: Contested figure: multiple published percentages for different years/methodologies given rather than a single number.

rows.claim: U.S. law enforcement estimated that Colombian money launderers send $5-15 billion in illicit drug proceeds from the United States back to Colombia annually, historically much of it via the Black Market Peso Exchange (BMPE), a trade-based laundering technique in which U.S. drug dollars are used to buy goods for Colombian importers, who pay pesos to the cartel without the cash ever crossing a border.
rows.sourceTitle: Laundering Colombia's drug money | Part 1: how to do it, Colombia Reports

rows.claim: HSBC paid a then-record $1.9 billion settlement in December 2012 for anti-money-laundering failures, admitting it had allowed at least $881 million in transfers controlled by the Sinaloa Cartel and other Mexican trafficking groups to move through its accounts; the settlement comprised a $1.3 billion forfeiture and a $650 million civil fine, with no individual indictment.
rows.sourceTitle: 'Profoundly Sorry' HSBC Reaches $1.9B Settlement In Money-Laundering Case, NPR

rows.claim: Chinese underground money-exchange networks ('Operation Fortune Runner') helped the Sinaloa Cartel launder more than $50 million in drug proceeds (fentanyl, cocaine, methamphetamine) between 2019 and 2023, using a mirrored renminbi-for-dollars settlement system driven by Mexican currency restrictions on dollar deposits and Chinese capital-control limits on citizens moving money abroad.
rows.sourceTitle: How Mexican Cartel, Chinese nationals launder drug money together, NBC Los Angeles

rows.claim: Analysis of over 100 cryptocurrency dealers/brokers linked to cartel laundering shows more than $55.5 million flowing into their wallets since June 2019, concentrated mostly in 2022-2023, using primarily Bitcoin and the USDT stablecoin, with 'spinners' converting between cryptocurrencies across a network spanning dozens of countries to obscure fund origin.
rows.sourceTitle: Understanding the Use of Cryptocurrencies By Cartels, TRM Labs

rows.case: Golden Triangle and Afghan opium economies
rows.claim: UNODC estimated Afghanistan's overall opium economy (including export value) at roughly $2 billion in 2019 -- about one-third of the value of Afghanistan's licit agricultural output and about 10% of total GDP; a later estimate valued the opium economy at $1.4-2.7 billion in 2021, or 9-14% of national GDP.
rows.sourceTitle: An Unforced Error: How US Attempts to Suppress the Opium Trade Strengthened the Taliban, Modern War Institute at West Point
rows.note: Contested/time-varying figure across cited years.

rows.case: Golden Triangle and Afghan opium economies
rows.claim: Afghan opium farm-gate income totaled about $1.4 billion in 2011 (9% of GDP), $600 million in 2004 (13% of GDP), and $1.39 billion in 2017 (roughly 7% of GDP) -- showing the opium economy's share of GDP falling even as absolute dollar values fluctuated.
rows.sourceTitle: Afghan opium prices soar as production rises, UNODC

rows.claim: In 2007 Purdue Frederick Co. pleaded guilty to a felony charge of illegally misbranding OxyContin, and Purdue together with three executives agreed to pay a total of $634.5 million (commonly cited as '$600 million').
rows.sourceTitle: Purdue Frederick plea agreement documents, U.S. Department of Justice

rows.claim: A 2021 multistate bankruptcy settlement required Purdue and the Sackler family to pay more than $5.5 billion, but in June 2024 the U.S. Supreme Court invalidated the deal, ruling the bankruptcy court could not grant the Sacklers a blanket liability shield from opioid-victim lawsuits.
rows.sourceTitle: Purdue Pharma opioid settlement that shielded Sackler family rejected by Supreme Court, CNN

rows.claim: Following the Supreme Court's 2024 ruling, a new $7.4 billion settlement in principle was reached in 2025 (the largest opioid settlement to date), with the Sackler family paying the bulk -- $6.5 billion over 15 years per one account, or an initial $1.5 billion plus staged payments of $500m/$500m/$400m per another account -- and Purdue paying nearly $900 million up front; the deal bars the Sacklers from ever selling opioids in the U.S. again and ends their control of the company.
rows.sourceTitle: AG Skrmetti and Bipartisan Coalition of 15 States Secure $7.4 Billion from Purdue Pharma and Sackler Family, Tennessee Attorney General
rows.note: Contested internal breakdown: two different payment-schedule breakdowns appear across sources; both given.

rows.claim: Under the 2025 settlement, approximately 9,300 local governments opted in, and New York State alone is set to receive up to $250 million.
rows.sourceTitle: Attorney General James Secures Approval of Purdue Bankruptcy Plan, New York Attorney General

rows.claim: FinCEN issued a formal advisory and financial-trend analysis on Chinese money-laundering networks, describing their role laundering fentanyl and precursor-trade proceeds for Mexican cartels as a distinct, growing typology of trade-based and underground-banking laundering.
rows.sourceTitle: FinCEN Issues Advisory and Financial Trend Analysis on Chinese Money Laundering Networks, U.S. Department of the Treasury/FinCEN

rows.case: British East India Company opium trade / Opium Wars
rows.claim: The number of opium smokers in China grew from about 12 million around the time of the First Opium War (1839-1842) to about 40 million by the 1880s, as lower-grade opium extended a habit once confined to wealthy merchants and officials into the middle and lower classes.
rows.sourceTitle: Objects of Addiction: Opium, Empire, and the Chinese Art Trade, Harvard Art Museums

rows.claim: The U.S. crack epidemic was triggered by a supply-side glut: cocaine powder flooding through the Bahamas/Dominican Republic caused prices to fall by as much as 80%, prompting dealers to convert powder into smokable 'crack' sold in small, cheap dosage units -- as little as $2.50 per unit in cities including New York, Philadelphia, Houston, Los Angeles and Detroit, versus $100 per gram for powder cocaine.
rows.figure: 80 percent price fall; $2.50 per crack dose vs $100/gram powder
rows.sourceTitle: The Crack Cocaine Epidemic That Devastated America, Into the Shadows

rows.claim: Around 1984, street cocaine powder averaged 55% purity at $100 per gram, while crack was sold at purity levels above 80% for the same price -- a purity-per-dollar innovation that helped the new product form spread to 28 states and the District of Columbia by the end of 1986.
rows.sourceTitle: Crack epidemic in the United States, Wikipedia

rows.claim: By 2000, Purdue had doubled the size of its sales force in pursuit of a roster of 70,000 'committed' physicians who would prescribe OxyContin for chronic non-cancer pain; reps were expected to make about 35 physician calls per week.
rows.sourceTitle: The history of OxyContin, told through Purdue Pharma documents, STAT

rows.claim: Purdue's sales-rep bonus structure was calculated to reward higher-dose prescribing: in 2001 average base salary was $55,000 versus an average annual bonus of $71,500, so total average rep income including bonus exceeded $120,000 -- with bonuses higher for OxyContin sales than for the company's other opioid, MS Contin.
rows.sourceTitle: New Court Documents Reveal OxyContin Manufacturer's Marketing Tactics, NPR

rows.claim: Internal memos instructed reps to 'Sell, Sell, Sell OxyContin' and to promote it for a widening range of pain conditions; a former sales representative alleges Purdue continued using deceptive 'pseudoaddiction' messaging (claiming apparent addiction symptoms meant patients needed higher doses, not less) even after its 2007 guilty plea.
rows.sourceTitle: Purdue Pharma used deceptive sales tactic for OxyContin after settlement, ex-sales rep says, CBS News

rows.claim: Fentanyl and its analogues have spread as adulterants mixed into heroin, cocaine, and methamphetamine supplies -- in some markets replacing heroin outright; about 69% of all U.S. drug overdose deaths in 2023 involved synthetic opioids other than methadone (chiefly illicit fentanyl).
rows.sourceTitle: Fentanyl, CDC Overdose Prevention

rows.claim: U.S. overdose deaths fell 27% from 110,037 in 2023 to 80,391 in 2024; researchers attribute a substantial part of the decline to reduced fentanyl potency/purity in the illicit supply ('the fentanyl hypothesis'), contemporaneous with DEA-measured drops in fentanyl purity.
rows.sourceTitle: Decreased Fentanyl Potency as the Primary Driver of the 2024 Decline in U.S. Overdose Deaths, medRxiv preprint

rows.case: British East India Company opium trade / Opium Wars
rows.claim: Queen Elizabeth I's 1600 royal charter gave the East India Company a 21-year trade monopoly plus sovereign-style powers: authority to make laws and impose penalties on offenders (so long as not repugnant to English law), to raise its own military forces, wage war, mint coin, negotiate treaties, and administer justice within its territories.
rows.sourceTitle: East India Company, EBSCO Research Starters

rows.case: British East India Company opium trade / Opium Wars
rows.claim: Opium made up less than 9% of British India's total revenue from 1792-1856, but by the time of independence in 1947 opium revenue had grown to outstrip customs duties, alcohol taxes, stamp charges, and income tax, second only to taxes on salt and land.
rows.sourceTitle: Opium in India: was the British Raj based on drug trading?, History Reclaimed

rows.case: British East India Company opium trade / Opium Wars
rows.unit: GBP net revenue per fiscal year
rows.sourceTitle: The Economic Importance of Indian Opium and Trade with China, Whitman College Working Paper 25

rows.claim: The phrase 'plata o plomo' ('silver or lead') originated with Pablo Escobar and the Medellín Cartel as an ultimatum to public officials -- accept a bribe (plata) or be killed (plomo, i.e. bullets) -- and has since become a named object of political-economy research on bribery, corruption, and violence against officials.
rows.sourceTitle: 'Plata o Plomo?': Bribe and Punishment in a Theory of Political Influence, American Political Science Review

rows.claim: Pablo Escobar's 'Medellín sin Tugurios' ('Medellín without Slums') housing program, launched 1984, built roughly 2,800 homes housing about 12,700 people for the city's poorest residents, funded with drug-trafficking money, and helped cement his popular image as a benefactor ('Colombian Robin Hood') in some communities.
rows.sourceTitle: Barrio Pablo Escobar: where Colombia's most infamous drug lord lives on, Colombia Reports

rows.claim: Escobar was elected as an alternate member of Colombia's Congress in 1982, using the office's parliamentary immunity as protection against extradition, before Justice Minister Rodrigo Lara-Bonilla exposed the illicit origin of his wealth and forced his resignation; Lara-Bonilla was assassinated months later.
rows.sourceTitle: Pablo Escobar Profile, InSight Crime

rows.claim: The Cali Cartel distinguished itself from Medellín's centralized, violently confrontational model by operating as a set of independent, cooperating criminal organizations run 'more on the model of a multinational corporation than a criminal enterprise,' with cartel leaders posing as legitimate businessmen and favoring low-profile operation over open war with the state.
rows.sourceTitle: The Cali Cartel, U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration

rows.claim: In Badiraguato and other poor mountain municipalities of Sinaloa, traffickers built churches, roads, and brought electricity to villages the government had neglected, cultivating reputations as benevolent patrons; supporters explicitly credit the cartel with providing jobs ('We support Chapo Guzmán because he is the one who gives us jobs and helps out in the mountains').
rows.sourceTitle: Narcoculture in Mexico, EBSCO Research Starters

rows.claim: An unspoken social pact existed in Culiacán between residents and the Sinaloa Cartel -- civilians tolerated cartel presence provided violence stayed off public streets; the October 2019 'Culiacanazo' incident (when security forces briefly detained then released Ovidio Guzmán amid armed cartel response) was widely reported as the moment that pact visibly broke down.
rows.sourceTitle: In a drug cartel hub, a social pact breaks, Los Angeles Times (via PressReader)

rows.case: Golden Triangle and Afghan opium economies
rows.claim: The Taliban taxes opium at every stage of the chain under Islamic-derived levies: a 10% 'ushr' harvest tax at the farm gate (yielding an estimated $44 million from about $440 million in gross farmer opium revenue), a 2.5% 'zakat' wealth tax, and additional 10% taxes on processing labs and traders moving product out of the country; overall Taliban tax revenue (opium and other) was estimated at about $160 million per year under Mullah Yaqoob's finance oversight.
rows.figure: 10 (ushr); 2.5 (zakat); 44 million (Taliban opium tax take); 160 million (total tax revenue)
rows.sourceTitle: How Opium Profits the Taliban, United States Institute of Peace

rows.case: Golden Triangle and Afghan opium economies
rows.claim: During the Vietnam War, the CIA-run 'Air America' airline flew weapons to anti-communist Hmong militias in Laos and, according to historian Alfred McCoy's research (initially denied by the U.S. State Department but subsequently corroborated by further scholarship), returned carrying raw opium out of cultivation areas, later refined into heroin in Saigon laboratories for export.
rows.sourceTitle: CIA drug trafficking allegations, Wikipedia (summarizing Alfred McCoy's 'The Politics of Heroin in Southeast Asia')
rows.note: McCoy's original allegations were contested by the State Department at the time; source notes subsequent scholarly research has documented the connections.

rows.case: Golden Triangle and Afghan opium economies
rows.claim: The Taliban banned opium poppy cultivation in April 2022 as a matter of state policy, a governance action credited with the sharp declines in Afghan cultivation and production measured in UNODC's subsequent surveys (down to 10,200 hectares / 296 tons by 2025).
rows.sourceTitle: Taliban bans drug cultivation, including lucrative opium, Al Jazeera

rows.claim: As part of the 2025 settlement, the Sackler family is permanently barred from manufacturing, selling, or marketing opioids in the United States and must give up control of Purdue, which is to be transferred to a non-profit entity (Knoa Pharma) -- a formal state-imposed withdrawal of the family's legitimacy to operate in the opioid business.
rows.sourceTitle: Purdue Pharma and Sackler Family Settlement in Principle, Connecticut Attorney General

rows.claim: The U.S. Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control has repeatedly sanctioned entities it identifies as part of the Sinaloa Cartel's global fentanyl and precursor supply network, including Chinese chemical suppliers, part of a governance response treating the trade as a sanctionable, narco-terrorism-linked network rather than ordinary narcotics crime.
rows.sourceTitle: Treasury Sanctions Global Illicit Drug Supply Chain Supporting the Sinaloa Cartel, U.S. Department of the Treasury

rows.claim: Historian David Courtwright's 'limbic capitalism' thesis (The Age of Addiction, Harvard University Press) explicitly places Purdue Pharma's opioid pills, McDonald's engineered food products, and Tencent's video games within one analytic category: 'a technologically advanced but socially regressive business system in which global industries, often with the help of complicit governments and criminal organizations, encourage excessive consumption and addiction' by targeting brain reward pathways.
rows.sourceTitle: Limbic Capitalism Has Been Driving Addiction for Hundreds of Years, After Babel (discussing David T. Courtwright's The Age of Addiction)
rows.note: This is the scholar's own claim, reported here as claim, not endorsed as fact by this research.

rows.claim: In August 2021, a newspaper affiliated with China's official Xinhua news agency labeled online gaming 'spiritual opium' (jingshen yapian) and 'electronic drugs,' echoing a term Chinese state media had used since 1961 to describe foreign cultural products as 'ideological poisoning worse than literal drugs'; the article triggered an 11% single-day stock drop in Tencent shares.
rows.sourceTitle: Video Games Are 'Spiritual Opium,' Says Chinese Government-Owned Media, Kotaku
rows.note: Reported as the scholarly/journalistic record of the state-media claim and its market effect, not as this research's own assessment of gaming's harms.

rows.claim: Critics and commentators have extended the 'spiritual opium' framing from video games to short-video platforms, describing them as 'electronic fentanyl,' 'electronic opium,' and 'electronic cocaine,' and warning of a potential new 'era of opium wars' driven by algorithmic engagement design.
rows.sourceTitle: Analysis of the causes, psychological mechanisms, and coping strategies of short video addiction in China, Frontiers in Psychology
rows.note: Stated as the cited commentators' framing, not this research's own conclusion.

rows.claim: Douyin (China's TikTok) built an 'adolescent mode' limiting minors to 40 minutes of viewing per day and blocking access from 10pm-6am, part of a broader Chinese regulatory response (including a February National Radio and Television Administration meeting on 'preventing underage users from becoming addicted') explicitly framed around platform-design addiction risk rather than the content itself.
rows.sourceTitle: How China takes extreme measures to keep teens off TikTok, MIT Technology Review

rows.claim: Marx's original 1843 phrase 'opium of the people,' referring to religion, has been academically re-examined (McKinnon, Critical Sociology, 2005) for its dialectical meaning in 19th-century pharmacology, and subsequently adopted by other commentators to characterize social media/Facebook as both a social 'safety valve' releasing unrest and a mechanism that keeps that unrest just contained enough to prevent structural change.
rows.sourceTitle: Reading 'Opium of the People': Expression, Protest and the Dialectics of Religion, Andrew M. McKinnon, Critical Sociology (2005)
rows.note: Original academic paper is about Marx's use of the metaphor for religion; the social-media application is a later, separate secondary-literature move, reported as such.

rows.claim: TikTok-focused platform scholarship explicitly analyzes the app within an 'attention economy'/'virality system' framework, arguing its algorithmic architecture is designed to keep users' 'eyeballs glued to the screen,' generating academic debate over the tension between commodification/visibility and authentic user experience.
rows.sourceTitle: TikTok and the algorithmic transformation of social media publics: From social networks to social interest clusters, Paolo Gerbaudo, New Media & Society

rows.claim: A published value-chain-analysis comparison of Colombian coffee and Colombian cocaine treats them as structurally comparable agricultural export chains grown under the same climatic/agricultural regimes for the same demand region (global North stimulant consumption) -- differing chiefly in legal status, not underlying commodity-chain structure -- directly supporting the claim that farm-to-distant-market logistics/financial technology in the cocaine trade is largely a general commodity-chain technology, not a narcotic-specific one.
rows.sourceTitle: Spatialising illicit commodity chains: Comparing coffee and cocaine, NSF Public Access Repository
rows.note: This is the cited scholars' argument, reported as their claim.

rows.claim: Scholars analyzing opium/heroin and cocaine markets find that most profit accrues to trafficking and wholesale distribution activities rather than to farm-level production, meaning drug-trafficking organizations generally have little incentive to invest resources controlling the (fungible, geographically dispersed, low-value-added) production stage -- a structural feature these scholars treat as general to illicit-commodity distribution economics rather than specific to any one narcotic.
rows.sourceTitle: Comparative Analysis of Illicit Supply Network Structure and Operations: Cocaine, Wildlife, and Sand, Journal of Illicit Economies and Development (LSE)
rows.note: Notably this paper's title itself compares cocaine trafficking structure to wildlife and (construction) sand trafficking -- explicitly non-narcotic illicit commodities -- as a test of general versus drug-specific network structure.

rows.claim: A value-chain study of the hashish supply to Europe found end-user prices increase by roughly 7,000% over production cost, a markup structure the authors analyze using generic value-chain-analysis methodology borrowed from legal-commodity supply-chain research, treating the extreme markup as a function of risk/enforcement economics general to prohibited-goods distribution rather than a property of cannabis specifically.
rows.sourceTitle: Understanding the illegal drug supply chain structure: a value chain analysis of the supply of hashish to Europe, Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (Nature)

rows.claim: Fentanyl's supply chain replaces an agrarian/geographically-fixed cultivation stage (required for opium and coca) with a portable, relocatable industrial chemistry stage; the same DEA/CRS reporting that documents Chinese precursor exporters shifting operations after 2019 PRC scheduling shows the industrial stage of the chain can be geographically reorganized far faster than a plant-based narcotic's growing regions could be -- illustrating that 'where value is added' (industrial vs. agrarian) is separable from which narcotic is involved.
rows.sourceTitle: China Primer: Illicit Fentanyl and China's Role, Congressional Research Service
rows.note: Interpretation drawn by this research from the cited report's documented facts, not a claim the report states in these exact separability terms.

rows.case: British East India Company opium trade / Opium Wars
rows.claim: The East India Company's specific governance technology -- compelled/monopsony cultivation (fixed-price purchase enforced through loans and exclusive delivery obligations to Company warehouses) combined with formal state-delegated sovereign powers (military force, treaty-making, taxation) -- is a general technology of colonial commodity extraction, independently attested in EIC administrative history outside the opium trade (e.g., its earlier and broader trade monopolies and territorial administration in India), not a technology unique to narcotics.
rows.sourceTitle: Corporate Sovereign Awakening and the Making of Modern State Sovereignty: New Archival Evidence from the English East India Company, International Organization (Cambridge Core)
rows.note: Interpretation: the cited article documents the EIC's general sovereign-corporate governance structure across its whole trade portfolio, of which opium was one commodity among several (textiles, tea, saltpeter); the separability claim is this research's synthesis of that fact, not the article's own stated framing.

rows.claim: Analysts and the DEA-adjacent trade press explicitly describe the Sinaloa Cartel's plaza system using ordinary corporate-franchise vocabulary ('subsidiary,' comparisons to Walmart and McDonald's), treating territorial franchising with a percentage remitted to central leadership as a known general organizational-design technology for scaling a decentralized, discovery-resistant distribution operation, applicable independent of which product (drugs, counterfeit goods, extortion) is being distributed.
rows.sourceTitle: Journal of Strategic Security, Volume 15 Number 4, University of South Florida

rows.claim: Colombia's National Comprehensive Substitution Program enrolled 99,097 farming families, promising each about $12,000 in cash assistance plus technical support to switch coca fields to legal crops, at a total government investment of $340 million intended to benefit 50,000 families; a late-2019 UNODC estimate found only 0.4% of enrolled farmers had actually replanted coca, and Colombian coca cultivation still rose 13% (from about 204,000 to 230,000 hectares) between December 2021 and December 2022.
rows.figure: 99,097 (families enrolled); 12,000 (USD per family); 340 million (USD program cost); 0.4 (percent replanted); 13 (percent cultivation increase)
rows.sourceTitle: A Death Foretold: Colombia's Crop Substitution Program, InSight Crime

rows.claim: Estimates of the cost to eradicate a single hectare of coca in Colombia vary enormously by method and who is counting: Colombia's Defense Ministry put glyphosate aerial-spraying eradication cost at just $800/hectare, while other estimates ranged from $25,000 to as much as $70,000 per hectare once military deployment, fuel, logistics and area-evacuation costs are included.
rows.sourceTitle: The Costs of Restarting Aerial Coca Spraying in Colombia, Washington Office on Latin America (WOLA)
rows.note: Contested figure: multiple published per-hectare estimates given because they use very different cost-accounting boundaries.

rows.claim: Americans spent on the order of $150 billion on cocaine, heroin, marijuana, and methamphetamine in 2016 (fluctuating between $120-145 billion across 2006-2016), a total RAND says rivals U.S. spending on alcohol -- a demand-side scale figure against which fentanyl's much lower per-dose retail price ($10-20/pill) and higher potency function as a competitive-pricing strategy within that overall market.
rows.unit: USD per year (all-drug U.S. retail spending)
rows.sourceTitle: Americans' Spending on Illicit Drugs Nears $150 Billion Annually; Appears to Rival What Is Spent on Alcohol, RAND Corporation

rows.claim: Estimates of Mexican drug-trafficking organizations' total annual revenue vary widely: one figure cites $35-45 billion annually with an approximate 80% profit margin; a separate U.S. State Department-derived estimate puts total drug-industry earnings at $14-48 billion annually -- a very wide, contested range reflecting the difficulty of measuring an illicit sector.
rows.sourceTitle: Reducing Drug Trafficking Revenues and Violence in Mexico, RAND Corporation
rows.note: Contested figure spanning a wide range across cited secondary sources; case relabeled 'Cross-case context' because the underlying RAND paper does not isolate a single Sinaloa-specific number, addressing the Mexican trade in aggregate.

rows.case: Golden Triangle and Afghan opium economies
rows.claim: Academic and DEA-adjacent risk-pricing research (Caulkins and Reuter) estimates that over 50% of the retail price of cocaine (and, by the same risk-compensation logic applied to opiates, of heroin) is attributable to compensation for the risks traffickers and dealers bear -- enforcement, detection, seizure, and violence -- rather than to production or refining cost; cocaine and heroin are, gram for gram, worth more than gold.
rows.unit: percent of retail price attributable to risk compensation
rows.sourceTitle: What Price Data Tell Us about Drug Markets, Jonathan P. Caulkins and Peter Reuter, Journal of Drug Issues (1998)
rows.note: Figure originates from cocaine-specific research (Caulkins and Reuter 1996) and is applied here by extension to the general opiate-refining risk-pricing logic; treat the >50% figure as specific to cocaine unless a parallel heroin-specific estimate is later found.

rows.claim: Interviews with a sample of Italian drug traffickers found retail-level markup of 121%, wholesale-level markup of 57%, and high-level multi-kilogram trafficker markup of only 26% -- showing markup concentrated overwhelmingly at the final retail repackaging stage of the industrial/distribution chain, a pattern researchers treat as general across drug types including opioids.
rows.sourceTitle: Uncertainty and risk: A framework for understanding pricing in online drug markets, International Journal of Drug Policy (ScienceDirect)

rows.claim: U.S. opioid-involved overdose deaths rose roughly tenfold over 1999-2023, from single-digit-thousands in the late 1990s to a peak of more than 81,800 deaths in 2022 (81,806 in 2022, declining to 79,358 in 2023) -- the human-toll backdrop against which the legal-industry settlements (2007, 2021, 2025) were negotiated as a form of after-the-fact state-imposed accountability rather than upfront prohibition.
rows.sourceTitle: Opioid Overdose Deaths: National Trends and Variation by Demographics and States, KFF
